results.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
results.proof_sketch: The sparse bound is at most n√m exactly when m^(4/3)≤n√m, equivalently m^(5/6)≤n, or m≤n^(6/5). The dense bound n² is at most a polylogarithmic multiple of n√m when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n. The ratio min{n²,m^(4/3)}/(n√m) is maximized where n²=m^(4/3), namely m=n^(3/2), and there equals n^(1/4).

results.claim: Balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, and either the insertion closes a cycle or the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological. Moreover, all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
results.proof_sketch: List descendants of v in increasing old topological order as f₁,f₂,… and ancestors of u in decreasing order as b₁,b₂,…, restricted to [v,u]. Expand these lists in pairs while fᵢ<bᵢ. If the searches intersect, or an explored edge joins their reached regions, there is an old v-to-u path. Otherwise let q be the number of pairs expanded. The next frontiers satisfy b_(q+1)<f_(q+1). Hence a cut exists strictly between max{f_q,b_(q+1)} and min{b_q,f_(q+1)}. The first q vertices of each list are precisely F and B for this cut. Moving B before F is safe: F has no edge to L\F by descendant closure; R\B has no edge to B by ancestor closure; an edge F→B would give an old v-to-u path; all other potentially reversed edges contradict the old topological order. Finally b reaches u and v reaches f for every b∈B,f∈F, so u→v creates b→u→v→f. Previously f<c<b, precluding b reaching f.

results.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
results.proof_sketch: For the ith violating acyclic insertion let |F_i|=|B_i|=q_i. By the lemma, q_i² distinct ordered vertex pairs become reachable for the first time. Reachability is monotone under insertion, so Σ_i q_i²≤n(n−1). Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σ_i q_i≤√(mΣ_iq_i²)=O(n√m). Min/max heaps enumerate the forward and backward searches in topological order; an implicit balanced sequence tree performs the stable extraction and reinsertion of F_i,B_i in Õ(q_i) time. Scanning adjacency lists contributes exactly A up to logarithmic heap overhead. Thus the stated bound follows. If the relevant direction-degree is polylogarithmic, A≤Õ(Σ_iq_i)=Õ(n√m).

results.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
results.proof_sketch: Use vertices v,z,u₁,…,u_r,w₁,…,w_r in initial order v,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r. First insert v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z for every i,j; all are order-consistent. Then insert u_i→v for i=1,…,r. Just before this insertion, v immediately precedes the remaining u_i's, v's r out-neighbors all lie after u_i, and u_i has no predecessor. Thus paired search selects only F={v}, B={u_i}, after which moving u_i immediately before v restores the order. Vertex u_i already reaches every w_j through z, so the only new reachability relation is u_i→v. Nevertheless, expanding v by rescanning its ordinary adjacency list examines r entries on each of r updates. Hence this implementation takes Ω(r²)=Ω(m²), versus n√m=Θ(r^(3/2)). This is an obstruction to that implementation, not a lower bound against smarter adjacency access.

final_writeup:
This does not resolve the arbitrary-degree problem. It does isolate a clean n√m ordering argument and the remaining adjacency-access bottleneck.

Assume distinct edge insertions and that the structure either maintains an implicit topological order while the graph is acyclic or reports the first cycle. Maintain the order in a balanced sequence tree. An insertion u→v is harmless when u precedes v. Otherwise search the old graph, excluding the new edge, forward from v and backward from u inside the old interval [v,u]. Forward-discovered vertices are held in increasing-order priority; backward-discovered vertices in decreasing-order priority. While the two frontier vertices f,b satisfy f<b, expand one from each side. A vertex discovered by both searches certifies an old v-to-u path.

If the frontiers cross without such a certificate, suppose q vertices were expanded on each side. The ordering of the searches yields a gap c for which the expanded forward set F is exactly the set of descendants of v at or left of c, while the expanded backward set B is exactly the set of ancestors of u right of c. Write L and R for all vertices at or left, respectively right, of c. Replace the old order by

(L minus F), B, F, (R minus B),

preserving the old order within every displayed set. Descendant and ancestor closure rule out newly reversed edges into L minus F or B. An old edge from F to B would produce a v-to-u path and hence a cycle. All remaining possible reversed directions contradict the old topological order. The new edge goes from u∈B to v∈F, so the resulting order is topological.

Every b∈B lay after every f∈F before the update, but afterward b reaches f through b→…→u→v→…→f. Thus q² ordered pairs become reachable for the first time. These pairs are disjoint between updates, giving Σq_i²≤n(n−1), and therefore Σq_i=O(n√m). Consequently, priority-queue and order-maintenance work associated with affected vertices already has the desired total bound.

Let A denote the total number of outgoing entries inspected while expanding forward vertices plus incoming entries inspected while expanding backward vertices. The direct implementation therefore costs Õ(m+n√m+A). This proves the target for the precisely scoped class A=Õ(n√m), including the stated low relevant-direction-degree condition.

The explicit v,z,u_i,w_j construction shows why the general conclusion does not follow: A can be quadratic even though q=1 and only one reachability relation is created at every bad insertion. A successful full proof therefore needs an adjacency mechanism that skips repeatedly irrelevant neighbors, or a different search/reordering rule; the reachability-pair potential alone cannot justify ordinary full-list scans.

Independently, the two bounds recorded in the permitted source cover m≤n^(6/5) and the near-dense regime m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n. The remaining polynomial gap is the intermediate-density, unrestricted-adjacency case.
checks_performed: Parsed only the specified JSON and its incremental-topological-sort section; no web or other repository files were accessed.

Exhaustively enumerated all DAG edge subsets consistent with a fixed topological order for n≤5. Across 4,100 non-cycle violating insertions, checked the cut identities, validity of the reordered topological order, and freshness of every B×F relation.
Across 6,550 cycle-forming cases for n≤5, checked that the paired search has an intersection or explored crossing-edge certificate before a cycle-free cut could be returned.
Simulated the obstruction family for r=1,2,3,5,10,25,100, verifying n=2r+2, m=4r, q=1 on every violating update, exactly one new reachability relation per such update, and r² adjacency scans.
All computational checks were exact and in-memory; the repository was not modified. The permitted temporary directory could not be created because the filesystem was read-only.
